questions.q: Why does OFFSET-based pagination get slower as the offset grows?
options: Later pages are stored on slower disk segments than earlier pages
Each page request must reopen and re-authenticate the database connection
The engine scans and discards every row before the requested offset
Deep pages bypass the buffer pool, forcing reads straight from disk
questions.explanation: OFFSET is not a seek: the engine still walks and throws away every row before the offset, so cost grows linearly with page depth regardless of storage layout.

questions.q: How does keyset pagination fetch the next page?
options: Filter rows beyond the last seen sort-key value, then apply a limit
Skip a row count computed from the page number, then apply a limit
Look up precomputed page boundaries stored in a separate mapping table
Re-run the full query and slice the desired page in application code
questions.explanation: Keyset pagination turns each page into a range predicate on the sort key (WHERE key > last_seen ... LIMIT n), letting the index seek straight to the start of the page.

questions.q: Why should a keyset-paginated query sort on a unique column or add a tiebreaker?
options: Unique columns compress better, which keeps encoded cursor payloads small
The optimizer refuses to use indexes on non-unique sorting columns
Unique sorts let the database parallelize the scan across many workers
Ties make ordering ambiguous, so rows can repeat or vanish across pages
questions.explanation: Without a unique tiebreaker the order among equal keys is undefined, so the cursor boundary can land mid-tie and duplicate or drop those rows between pages.

questions.q: A user pages through a feed while new items are inserted. With OFFSET pagination, what happens?
options: The database blocks new inserts until the paginating session closes
Rows shift across page boundaries, so items repeat or get skipped
The offset is recalculated automatically to keep pages consistent
New items are held in a staging area until the session ends
questions.explanation: An offset counts positions in a moving result set. Inserts push existing rows down, so the next page starts at a shifted position and items repeat or get skipped.

questions.q: What does an opaque pagination cursor typically encode?
options: A server-side session ID pointing at a stored result snapshot
The complete SQL text of the query that generated the previous page
The sort-key values of the last row returned on the previous page
A checksum of every row already delivered to the client
questions.explanation: The cursor carries the position in the sort order, i.e. the last row's sort-key values, so the server can rebuild the range predicate for the next page without server state.

questions.q: Why do APIs return opaque, encoded cursors instead of raw column values?
options: Encoding compresses the cursor so responses stay under size limits
It hides internals so clients can't tamper and the format can evolve
Raw values would leak the database engine's version to attackers
Opaque cursors are required by the HTTP specification for list endpoints
questions.explanation: Opacity keeps the cursor an implementation detail: clients treat it as a blob they echo back, so the server can change sort keys or encoding without breaking them.

questions.q: Which pagination style suits an infinite-scroll feed best?
options: Offset pagination, because page numbers map directly to scroll position
Random sampling, because feeds don't need a deterministic order
Server-side HTML pagination with numbered links rendered per request
Cursor pagination, since it stays fast and stable as items arrive
questions.explanation: Infinite scroll only ever asks for "what comes after this", which is exactly a cursor seek: constant cost per page and no shifting when new items are inserted at the head.

questions.q: What ability do you give up when moving from OFFSET to keyset pagination?
options: Jumping directly to an arbitrary page number
Sorting results by any indexed column
Returning consistent page sizes to the client
Paginating tables larger than available memory
questions.explanation: A cursor names a position in the sort order, not an ordinal page, so you can only walk forward or backward from a known row rather than jump to page N.

questions.q: An API sorts by created_at only, and many rows share timestamps. Pages sometimes skip rows. What's the fix?
options: Add a unique column like id as a secondary sort key inside the cursor
Increase the page size so ties always fall inside a single page
Switch the timestamp column to millisecond precision instead
Cache each page server-side so repeated requests return identical rows
questions.explanation: Adding id makes the sort key totally ordered, so the (created_at, id) comparison resumes exactly where the last page ended instead of skipping the rest of a tie group.

questions.q: A dashboard needs 'go to page 47 of 3,000'. Which approach fits?
options: Keyset pagination with cursors chained from page 1 up to page 47
Streaming the full result set and discarding rows client-side
A separate search cluster that materializes each page as a document
OFFSET pagination, accepting the scan cost for random page access
questions.explanation: Random page access is exactly what OFFSET gives you and cursors do not. For bounded admin-style result sets the scan cost is an acceptable price for jump-to-page.

questions.q: Your cursor encodes {last_id: 900}. Row 900 is deleted before the next request. What does a well-built keyset query do?
options: Fails with a 410 Gone error because the anchor row can no longer be found
Works fine, since it filters on values, not the anchor row's existence
Restarts from the first page to rebuild a consistent snapshot
Returns an empty page until the client requests a fresh cursor
questions.explanation: The query is a range predicate like id > 900; it never looks the anchor row up, so deleting it changes nothing about which rows follow that boundary value.

questions.q: Search results use offset pagination over lagging replicas. Users see duplicates across pages. Why?
options: Replicas rebuild their indexes on read, temporarily reordering rows
The load balancer caches page one and serves it for later offsets
Different replicas see different data, so offsets point at shifted rows
Offset queries bypass replicas and race against the primary's writes
questions.explanation: An offset is only meaningful against one consistent snapshot. Routing successive pages to replicas at different replication positions shifts row positions, so rows repeat.

questions.q: You must paginate a feed ranked by a score that changes between requests. What's a common practical approach?
options: Snapshot the ranking (score and id at request time) into the cursor
Re-rank on every request and trust offsets to stay aligned
Lock the scoring job while any user is mid-pagination
Round all scores to integers so ordering changes less often between pages
questions.explanation: Freezing the ranking values in the cursor gives the pagination a stable frame of reference, so later pages stay consistent even as live scores drift underneath.

questions.q: An endpoint returns next_cursor even when no more rows exist, and clients loop forever. What's the standard fix?
options: Return HTTP 204 for every page after the first empty one
Have clients stop after a fixed maximum number of pages
Fetch limit+1 rows; only emit a cursor when an extra row exists
Encode the total row count into every cursor for client-side checks
questions.explanation: Reading one extra row cheaply proves whether a next page exists. Return only limit rows and omit the cursor when the extra row is absent, giving clients a real terminator.

questions.q: Cursors your API issued last month break after you rename an internal sort column. What practice would have prevented client-visible failures?
options: Storing cursors client-side in localStorage with an expiry timestamp
Publishing the internal cursor format so clients could migrate stored values themselves
Using shorter cursor strings so old values remained parseable
Versioning the cursor payload and keeping decode support for old versions
questions.explanation: A version tag lets the server recognize old payloads and translate them to the new schema, so long-lived cursors keep working across internal changes.

questions.q: For a keyset query filtering (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ordered by both descending, which index serves it best?
options: A hash index on id, since the tiebreaker drives the lookup
A composite B-tree index on (created_at, id) matching the sort order
Separate single-column indexes on created_at and on id
A full-text index covering both columns to allow flexible range matching
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree in the same column order lets the engine seek to the tuple boundary and read rows already sorted, so no separate sort or merge of two indexes is needed.

questions.q: A public API gets scraped via deep pagination, causing heavy load. Which mitigation preserves legitimate use while cutting the scan cost?
options: Cap OFFSET at ten thousand and reject deeper requests with an error
Move to cursor pagination so every page is an index seek, then rate-limit
Add a CAPTCHA challenge before serving any page past the first
Shrink the page size so each individual request scans fewer rows
questions.explanation: Cursors make deep pages as cheap as the first, removing the quadratic scan cost entirely, while rate limits bound throughput without blocking real clients.

questions.q: Total-count display ('page 3 of 812') on a 500M-row filtered table is timing out. Which tradeoff do large systems usually pick?
options: Precompute exact counts for every possible filter combination nightly
Run COUNT(*) in a transaction at a higher isolation level for speed
Shard the table so each shard's count stays under the timeout
Show an estimate or 'many results' and drop exact deep counts
questions.explanation: Exact counts over arbitrary filters require touching every matching row, so big systems relax the requirement and serve a cheap estimate that users barely notice.

questions.q: You paginate across shards by fanning out and merging. What must each shard request include so the merged stream stays correct?
options: The global cursor's sort-key bound, applied identically on every shard
The page number, so each shard can skip the same number of rows
A shard-local row offset tracked separately for every shard
The merged result of the previous page for deduplication on the shard
questions.explanation: Only a shared sort-key boundary defines the same global cut on every shard, so the merge resumes exactly after the last emitted row. Per-shard offsets drift apart immediately.

questions.q: A cursor API must tolerate the client retrying the same page request. Why are cursors naturally better here than offsets under concurrent writes?
options: Cursors take row-level locks on the underlying rows until the client acknowledges
Offsets are mutable server state, while cursors are stored in the database
The same cursor re-runs the same bounded query, so retries can't skip rows
Cursor requests are cached by the CDN, so retries never hit the database
questions.explanation: A cursor request is effectively idempotent: it re-issues a fixed range predicate anchored to a value, so a retry returns the same window instead of a position shifted by concurrent writes.
